title: Leadership Admired Leadership The Silent Career Derailer of Defensiveness
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article identifies defensiveness as a 'silent career derailer' -- a behavioural pattern that quietly limits advancement, particularly into senior leadership, yet rarely receives direct feedback because naming it tends to produce the very reaction it describes. Defensive leaders overreact to criticism, make excuses, blame others, and deflect feedback -- behaviours that erode trust, reduce coachability, and diminish a leader's ability to develop others. The article argues that defensiveness compounds: frequent small defensive reactions create a pattern that others notice long before the defensive person becomes aware, quietly capping their advancement. Leaders who wish to progress must develop the capacity to receive disagreement and unfavourable feedback without overreacting -- because defensiveness is viewed by senior leaders as a direct indicator of coachability and future potential. The piece ends with a sharp challenge: defensiveness is career self-sabotage disguised as self-protection, and it destroys influence.
points: * Defensiveness is among the chief reasons high-performing leaders are bypassed for promotion: it signals to senior leaders that a person is less coachable, less able to receive candid feedback, and less able to develop others. * The pattern is self-concealing: many defensive people never receive direct feedback about their defensiveness because naming it is likely to elicit a defensive reaction, making it a genuinely 'silent' derailer that accumulates across years without correction. * Common defensive behaviours -- making excuses, arguing every point, denying responsibility, overexplaining, blaming others, deflecting with sarcasm -- are individually recognisable but collectively devastating when they form a pattern. * Defensiveness blocks three things senior leadership requires: it impedes learning, prevents candid feedback (creating a feedback desert), and reduces accountability -- all compounding over time. * Defensiveness is career self-sabotage disguised as self-protection: the instinct that feels like protecting credibility in the moment is systematically destroying influence and reputation over time.
quotes: Highly defensive people overreact when others disagree with them or when they receive unfavorable news and feedback. This can be a career killer. People respond defensively in many ways, usually to protect themselves from evaluation, criticism, rejection, or loss of control.

Among the common expressions of defensiveness, the most annoying are making excuses, arguing every point, denying responsibility, and overexplaining decisions. Minimizing their own missteps, blaming others, and deflecting criticism with sarcasm or mockery are equally uncomfortable and irritating.

Frequent defensiveness is among the chief reasons people are overlooked for promotion. Without fully realizing how often they act defensively, these self-protective leaders and team members gradually erode the trust and confidence others have in them.

Defensiveness impedes learning, restricts the likelihood of receiving candid feedback, and reduces accountability when things go wrong. More importantly, defensive team members are viewed as less coachable and thereby less able to coach and develop others.

Unfortunately, many people who are regularly defensive never receive strong feedback about their dysfunctional style. Or if they do, the feedback is typically aimed at a specific episode rather than at an overall pattern. This makes defensiveness a silent derailer.
Ironically, telling a colleague that they have a defensive posture and style is likely to elicit a defensive reaction, so leaders often keep the feedback to themselves.
Defensiveness is career self-sabotage disguised as self-protection. It doesn't just block criticism. It destroys influence.
